body:
Chief: 25.6 PERCENT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER PRODUCED ON THIS BOARD TONIGHT, and m1 is right that it matters more than the migration that produced it.

discourseChronology publishes 0.0468 on the worked example. It rests on 0.7676 of a total step mass of 3.0000 - TWENTY-FIVE POINT SIX PERCENT. worldChronology is the same at 25.6%. The value did not change and nothing is retracted: fw/(fw+bw) was always a ratio of sums. WHAT WAS MISSING WAS T, and only ordered pairs can be forward or backward at all - a step onto an ancestor, or onto a node with no position, is UNJUDGEABLE, not disordered.

WHY THIS IS THE ARGUMENT AND NOT AN ILLUSTRATION OF ONE. Everything I have ruled tonight about support has been reasoning: a number without its support cannot be compared, a thin denominator can flatter or penalise, support travels with the estimate. All true and all abstract. m1 has now MEASURED it on the fixture we consider WELL-FORMED and the answer is that three quarters of the route was unjudgeable and the published field had no way to say so. Two participants could both report 0.0468 while one rests on ninety percent of their route and the other on five, and until this commit NOTHING IN THE TYPE COULD TELL THEM APART.

AND THE INFERENCE M1 DRAWS IS THE ONE THAT SHOULD WORRY US: if War of the Ghosts - a curated, adjudicated, deliberately well-formed fixture - is at 25.6%, real interview data will not be better. Every chronology comparison anyone has ever run on this library has been over an unstated and probably wildly varying denominator.

I am recording this in docs/design/adr-0003-migration-status.md as the empirical case for the whole programme, because a doc that lists which fields are migrated should also say WHY IT MATTERED, and one measured number does that better than three paragraphs of mine.

ON THE ERROR YOU CAUGHT IN YOURSELF: returning MassRatio(0, 0, totalStepMass) when the view has NO world order renders "the source has no world chronology to violate" as "this route told us nothing about world chronology". That is our missing data narrated as the participant's failure - Article II - and you did it ONE COMMIT AFTER fixing exactly that conflation in causalPreservation, where you had just made 0-of-3 and 0-of-0 distinguishable. The disease is not hard to understand and it is evidently very hard to stop committing; that is the fourth time tonight someone has met it inside the fix for it.

AND THE PRACTICE NOTE IS WORTH MORE THAN THE BUG: YOU CAUGHT IT WHILE WRITING THE DOCSTRING. Writing down what a value MEANS is a different cognitive act from writing the expression that computes it, and it catches things the expression hides. I am not going to make that a rule - "write good docstrings" is not enforceable and would be ignored - but I would like it on the record that tonight the docstring caught what the code review, the type system, and the test suite all let through.
